questions.question: Which distinction frames data-intensive work, and what is rarely the limiting factor?

options.text: Stateless vs stateful applications; network bandwidth is rarely limiting
Data-intensive vs compute-intensive applications; raw CPU power is rarely limiting
OLTP vs OLAP applications; disk capacity is rarely limiting
Monolithic vs distributed applications; memory is rarely limiting

questions.explanation: Many applications today are data-intensive, as opposed to compute-intensive. Raw CPU power is rarely a limiting factor for them.

questions.question: For data-intensive applications, which three things are the bigger problems? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The amount of data
The complexity of data
The cost of CPU cycles
The speed at which the data is changing

questions.explanation: Amount, complexity, and speed of change. Three separate growth axes — the scalability section's insistence on naming which dimension grows begins here.

questions.question: Which building block serves the need to remember the result of an expensive operation, to speed up reads?

options.text: Search indexes
Batch processing
Caches
Stream processing

questions.explanation: Caches. Note the precise wording: the need is about speeding up reads by remembering an expensive result, not about storage.

questions.question: A database stores data so that ______ can find it again later. Fill the blank.

options.text: you, the developer who wrote it
they, or another application,
the operations team on call
any user with the right permissions

questions.explanation: 'Store data so that they, or another application, can find it again later.' Persistence is for other programs too, not just for you.

questions.question: Why does the standard list of data-system building blocks sound 'painfully obvious'?

options.text: Because the list is deliberately simplified for readers new to data systems
Because most engineers have written a storage engine themselves at some point
Because the abstraction is so successful that we use these tools without thinking
Because vendors market these categories so heavily that everyone knows them

questions.explanation: A good abstraction's payoff is that it stops being visible as a choice: most engineers wouldn't dream of writing a new data storage engine from scratch, because databases are a perfectly good tool for the job.

questions.question: Having called the building blocks a successful abstraction, the chapter immediately raises two difficulties. Which two? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Choice — many systems with differing characteristics, because applications differ in requirements
Combination — tools must be stitched together when one cannot do the whole job alone
Cost — licensing fees for data tools dominate the budget of most projects
Staffing — too few engineers understand how storage engines actually work inside

questions.explanation: Choice and combination. The second drives what follows: combining tools is what produces a composite, special-purpose data system.

questions.question: A database and a message queue both store data for some time, yet the chapter calls them very different categories. Which two reasons does it give for lumping them together as 'data systems' anyway? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The boundaries between the categories have blurred
Both guarantee durability for every message they accept
Applications increasingly need several tools stitched together
Both expose the same delivery semantics to their clients

questions.explanation: Boundaries between categories have blurred, and applications increasingly need several tools stitched together to meet their requirements. Neither durability nor delivery semantics is the reason — those differ sharply between a database and a queue.

questions.question: You add a Memcached caching layer and an Elasticsearch server alongside your main database. Whose responsibility is it to keep them in sync?

options.text: The database's replication subsystem
The application code's
The cache's write-through policy
The operations team's monitoring

questions.explanation: The application code's. And that is the moment the chapter says you are now a data system designer.

questions.question: Once you combine several tools behind one API, what follows?

options.text: The weakest component's guarantees automatically propagate to the whole composite service
You can stop reasoning about the guarantees of the individual tools altogether
Overall performance becomes simply the sum of the components' performance
Your composite service makes guarantees of its own, making you a data system designer

questions.explanation: You have created a new, special-purpose data system from smaller, general-purpose components — and it carries guarantees of its own.

questions.question: Which concern does this define: 'Over time many different people will work on the system, and they should all be able to work on it productively'?

options.text: Reliability
Scalability
Maintainability
Operability

questions.explanation: Maintainability. Note it is defined in terms of people, not code — operability, simplicity and evolvability are its three sub-principles.

questions.question: What does reliability mean, compressed to a phrase?

options.text: Never failing under any circumstances
Continuing to work correctly, even when things go wrong
Recovering quickly after a failure
Meeting the agreed service level agreement

questions.explanation: 'Continuing to work correctly, even when things go wrong.' Reliability is not the absence of faults but correctness in their presence.

questions.question: The chapter lists four typical expectations that add up to 'working correctly'. Which one is the odd one out because it is not about correctness at all?

options.text: The application performs the function the user expected
It tolerates the user making mistakes or using the software in unexpected ways
Its performance is good enough under the expected load and data volume
The system prevents any unauthorized access and abuse

questions.explanation: Security. It is easy to forget in a list about correctness, yet the chapter includes it in what 'working correctly' means.

questions.question: Define fault and failure as the chapter does.

options.text: A fault is a user mistake; a failure is a hardware or network problem
A fault is transient and recoverable; a failure is permanent and needs repair
A fault is one component deviating from spec; a failure is the system stopping service
A fault is found by monitoring; a failure is reported to you by customers

questions.explanation: A fault is one component deviating from its spec; a failure is the system as a whole stopping to provide the required service to the user. The design conclusion: reducing the probability of faults to zero is the wrong target, so you build fault-tolerance mechanisms that prevent faults from causing failures.

questions.question: Why is the term 'fault-tolerant' slightly misleading?

options.text: Because tolerating a fault implies the fault was anticipated in the design
Because no system tolerates every kind of fault, so the claim must be scoped
Because it describes an aspiration that no real system has ever achieved
Because it comes from hardware engineering and misleads applied to software

questions.explanation: It only makes sense to talk about tolerating certain types of faults. Hence the black-hole remark: tolerating a black hole swallowing Earth would require web hosting in space.

questions.question: Why can it make sense to deliberately increase the rate of faults in a fault-tolerant system?

options.text: To keep rarely used error-handling code exercised, as Netflix's Chaos Monkey does
To lower the mean time to failure of the individual components
To produce the fault records that compliance audits require
To make high-percentile response time measurements more representative

questions.explanation: Many high-severity bugs are caused by poor error handling; deliberately triggering faults ensures the tolerance mechanism is continually tested rather than silently rotting.

questions.question: The chapter generally prefers tolerating faults to preventing them, but names an exception. Which, and what makes it exceptional?

options.text: Hardware faults, because they occur independently on each machine
Human error, because people remain the least predictable component
Software bugs, because the same bug is present on every node at once
Security, because a breach of sensitive data cannot afterwards be undone

questions.explanation: If an attacker has compromised a system and gained access to sensitive data, that event cannot be undone — so prevention is preferred there.

questions.question: Hard disks are reported to have an MTTF of about 10 to 50 years. On a storage cluster with 10,000 disks, what should you expect?

options.text: One disk to die per week
One disk to die per day
One disk to die per hour
One disk to die per month

questions.explanation: 10,000 disks at a 10-year MTTF gives about 2.7 deaths/day; at 50 years about 0.55/day. The chapter's 'on average one disk to die per day' sits inside that band.

questions.question: Which of these are hardware-redundancy measures? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Disks in a RAID configuration
Dual power supplies and hot-swappable CPUs
Batteries and diesel generators for backup power
Checksums in application code to detect corrupted records

questions.explanation: Checksums are a software measure, not hardware redundancy. The honest claim attached to the real three: they cannot completely prevent hardware problems from causing failures, but the approach is well understood and can often keep a machine running uninterrupted for years.

questions.question: Until recently, hardware redundancy alone sufficed for most applications. What exact condition did that argument depend on?

options.text: That the application served fewer than a hundred concurrent users
That you can restore a backup onto a new machine fairly quickly
That the disks were enterprise-grade rather than consumer models
That the datacenter had two fully independent power feeds

questions.explanation: Single-machine redundancy plus fast restore made full high availability unnecessary for most non-critical applications.

questions.question: Which two trends broke the 'hardware redundancy is enough' assumption? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Data volumes and appetite for computing grew, so more machines means more faults
Cloud platforms favour elasticity over single-machine reliability, so instances vanish
Disks became fundamentally less reliable than they were in the 1990s
Virtualization made single-machine failure rates impossible to measure

questions.explanation: AWS instances can become unavailable without warning. The software-fault-tolerance systems that replaced single-machine redundancy also bring an operational benefit: nodes can be patched one at a time, so a rolling upgrade needs no planned downtime.

questions.question: Along which axis do hardware faults differ from systematic software errors, and what follows?

options.text: Cost — software errors are cheaper to fix, so they matter less in practice
Detectability — software errors are always surfaced by monitoring
Correlation — software errors hit every node at once, causing more failures
Frequency — hardware faults occur far more often than software errors

questions.explanation: Software errors are correlated across nodes and so tend to cause many more system failures than uncorrelated hardware faults. Adding redundant nodes does not help against a bug present in every instance.

questions.question: Which incident is the canonical example of a systematic software error, with its date and cause?

options.text: The Y2K rollover of January 1, 2000, caused by two-digit year fields
The leap second of June 30, 2012, which hung applications via a Linux kernel bug
The AWS S3 outage of February 28, 2017, caused by a mistyped runbook command
The Knight Capital loss of August 1, 2012, caused by a stale deployment

questions.explanation: The other examples it gives are undated: a runaway process using up a shared resource, a service the system depends on slowing down or returning corrupted responses, and cascading failures.

questions.question: Why do systematic software bugs 'lie dormant for a long time' before firing?

options.text: They need unusual circumstances, and reveal an environmental assumption that stopped holding
They are introduced only during upgrades, so they fire on the next deployment after that
Compilers optimize them away entirely until the load rises above some threshold
They only trigger once the disk has filled up and writes have begun to fail

questions.explanation: Until then the software works fine. The leap-second bug's assumption was that time moves forward monotonically, one second per second.

questions.question: 'Design systems in a way that minimizes opportunities for error' is the first human-error mitigation. Which caveat comes with it?

options.text: That designing such interfaces costs far more than training people properly
That it works only for internal tools, not customer-facing interfaces
That over-restrictive interfaces get worked around, negating the benefit
That it must always be paired with a formal certification programme

questions.explanation: Well-designed abstractions, APIs and admin interfaces make it easy to do the right thing — but if the interfaces are too restrictive people will work around them. A tricky balance to get right.

questions.question: The chapter demands two properties of the sandbox where people can explore and experiment. Which? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Fully featured, so it exercises the real code paths
Using real data, so the behaviour observed is representative
Isolated on a separate physical network segment
Reset to a clean state automatically after every use

questions.explanation: Fully featured and using real data, but without affecting real users — that is what decouples the place mistakes are made from the place they cause failures.

questions.question: Which levels of testing are needed, and what is automated testing especially valuable for?

options.text: Unit tests only; valuable mainly as protection against regressions
Integration and load tests; valuable chiefly for catching performance regressions
Chaos tests only; valuable for validating that fault tolerance really works
Unit through whole-system integration plus manual tests; valuable for rare corner cases

questions.explanation: Automated testing is especially valuable for covering corner cases that rarely arise in normal operation. Manual tests are explicitly in the list — the chapter does not claim everything can be automated.

questions.question: Which three recovery mechanisms limit the impact of human error? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Fast rollback of configuration changes
Gradual rollout of new code, so bugs reach only a subset of users
Tools to recompute data, in case the old computation was incorrect
Mandatory review by a second engineer before any change ships

questions.explanation: Each buys a different kind of reversibility: config, code, and derived data. Peer review is not on this list.

questions.question: What do other engineering disciplines call monitoring, and what analogy fits?

options.text: Instrumentation, by analogy with the dashboard of a car
Telemetry, by analogy with a rocket that has left the ground
Auditing, by analogy with double-entry financial accounting
Observability, by analogy with a medical diagnostic scan

questions.explanation: Once a rocket has left the ground, telemetry is essential for tracking what is happening and for understanding failures. Its three distinct jobs: early warning signals, checking whether assumptions or constraints are being violated, and diagnosing after an incident.

questions.question: Which human-error mitigation lies outside the scope of a book on data systems?

options.text: Detailed and clear monitoring
Good management practices and training
Sandbox environments
Quick and easy recovery

questions.explanation: It calls them a complex and important aspect, and beyond the scope of the book.

questions.question: Under what circumstances may you consciously sacrifice reliability, and with what condition?

options.text: Never; the chapter treats reliability as non-negotiable in every system
Only where a signed SLA explicitly permits a lower level of service
To cut development or operational cost, provided we know we are cutting corners
Only for internal tools that have no external paying users

questions.explanation: Its examples are a prototype for an unproven market (development cost) and a service with a narrow profit margin (operational cost). Cutting corners is allowed; doing it unknowingly is not.

questions.question: How is scalability defined, and why are both 'X is scalable' and 'Y doesn't scale' meaningless?

options.text: Coping with increased load; the useful question is how to cope with a given growth
Maximum sustainable throughput; the phrases fail because throughput is mismeasured
The ability to add machines; the phrases fail because any system can add machines
Capacity rising linearly with cost; the phrases fail because cost is never linear

questions.explanation: Scalability is not a one-dimensional label, so the meaningful discussion is 'if the system grows in a particular way, what are our options for coping with the growth?' And: how can we add computing resources to handle the additional load?

questions.question: Why must load be described before growth can be discussed?

options.text: Because current load is far easier to measure than any future growth
Because 'what if load doubles?' is unanswerable without load parameters
Because the growth rate tells you how many machines to buy up front
Because the load figure dictates which database you ought to choose

questions.explanation: Load parameters come first; growth questions are meaningless without a succinct description of the current load.

questions.question: What determines the best choice of load parameters?

options.text: Published industry benchmarks for your class of application
Requests per second, which is the right parameter for every system
The guidance issued by your database vendor for that workload
Your architecture — the average case, or a few extreme cases, may dominate

questions.explanation: Perhaps the average case matters, or perhaps your bottleneck is dominated by a small number of extreme cases. Examples include requests per second to a web server, the ratio of reads to writes in a database, simultaneously active users in a chat room, and the hit rate on a cache.

questions.question: Twitter's November 2012 figures: post tweet and home timeline. Which pair is right, and where does the difficulty lie?

options.text: Post tweet 300k/sec, home timeline 4.6k/sec; the difficulty is write volume
Post tweet 4.6k/sec (12k peak), home timeline 300k/sec; the difficulty is fan-out
Post tweet 12k/sec, home timeline 45k/sec; the difficulty is storage volume
Post tweet 4.6k/sec, home timeline 30M/sec; the difficulty is network bandwidth

questions.explanation: Handling 12,000 writes/sec would be fairly easy. Twitter's scaling challenge is fan-out: each user follows many people and is followed by many people.

questions.question: Where is the term 'fan-out' borrowed from, and what does it mean in transaction processing systems?

options.text: Fluid dynamics; the way load spreads out across partitions
Electronic engineering; requests to other services per incoming request
Broadcast radio; the number of subscribers listening to one topic
Graph theory; the out-degree of a vertex in a directed graph

questions.explanation: In electronics it describes the number of logic gate inputs attached to one gate's output.

questions.question: Which metaphor fits approach 2 to Twitter's timeline problem?

options.text: A ledger of tweets, appended once per post and replayed on read
A firehose of tweets, sampled per user when a timeline is requested
A mailbox of tweets, one per recipient user, filled at write time
A ring buffer of tweets, overwritten as newer posts arrive

questions.explanation: A cache for each user's home timeline — like a mailbox of tweets for each recipient user. Approach 1 inserts into a global collection of tweets and joins at read time (expensive reads); approach 2 computes the timeline ahead of time, at write time.

questions.question: Give the quantitative reason Twitter moved from approach 1 to approach 2.

options.text: Published tweets run almost two orders of magnitude below timeline reads
Reads turned out to be two orders of magnitude cheaper than writes
Storage costs fell by two orders of magnitude, making precomputation free
Relational joins on the tweet table could not be indexed efficiently

questions.explanation: So it is preferable to do more work at write time and less at read time. 4.6k writes/sec versus 300k reads/sec is roughly a 65x gap, which the chapter rounds to almost two orders of magnitude.

questions.question: A tweet is delivered to about 75 followers on average. What write load does approach 2 create, and what is the worst case?

options.text: About 345k writes/sec; worst case over 30M writes for one tweet, within five seconds
About 345k writes/sec; worst case one million writes, within one minute
About 4.6k writes/sec; worst case 30M writes, within five minutes
About 12k writes/sec; worst case 300k writes, within one second

questions.explanation: 4.6k tweets/sec times 75 followers is about 345k writes/sec. The celebrity worst case — a user with over 30 million followers — is what the chapter calls a significant challenge, given its five-second delivery target.

questions.question: For Twitter, what is the key load parameter?

options.text: Tweets published per second, averaged out across the whole day
The distribution of followers per user, weighted by how often they tweet
The total number of accounts ever registered on the service
The ratio of timeline reads to tweet writes across the system

questions.explanation: The distribution matters, not the average — because it determines fan-out work. The weighting refinement makes it reflect actual write load.

questions.question: Describe the hybrid Twitter ended up with.

options.text: All timelines computed at read time, backed by an aggressive cache
Fan-out at write time for celebrities, and read-time joins for everyone else
Timelines sharded by follower count, so large accounts get dedicated machines
Fan-out at write time, except celebrities, whose tweets are merged on read

questions.explanation: Celebrities with very large numbers of followers are excepted from fan-out. Option b inverts it. This keeps the pathological case off the write path while preserving cheap reads for the common case.

questions.question: Once load is described, the chapter says you can investigate increased load in two ways. Which? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Increase a load parameter with resources unchanged, and ask how performance suffers
Ask how much you must add to resources to hold performance unchanged
Reduce the load parameter to zero and measure the system's idle cost
Compare your figures against a competitor's published benchmark

questions.explanation: Both questions require performance numbers, which is why the chapter turns next to throughput and response time.

questions.question: Which metric matters in a batch processing system such as Hadoop, and which in an online system?

options.text: Throughput for batch; response time for online
Response time for batch; throughput for online
Throughput for both
Availability for batch; latency for online

questions.explanation: Throughput is records processed per second, or total time to run a job on a dataset of a given size. Because of skew you have to wait for the slowest task to complete.

questions.question: Distinguish latency from response time. Which one does the client see?

options.text: They are synonyms, and both describe what the client observes
Response time is what the client sees; latency is time spent awaiting service
Latency is what the client sees; response time is measured only server-side
Response time is the median; latency is the 99th percentile of the same data

questions.explanation: Response time is service time plus network delays and queueing delays. Latency is the duration a request is waiting to be handled — latent, awaiting service. Conflating the two is one of the chapter's named precision traps.

questions.question: Which causes make response times vary, even for identical repeated requests? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: A context switch to a background process
Loss of a network packet and TCP retransmission, or a garbage collection pause
A page fault forcing a read from disk, or mechanical vibrations in the server rack
Variation in the CPU's advertised clock speed rating

questions.explanation: Because of all this, response time must be thought of as a distribution of values, not a single number.

questions.question: What is the objection to reporting average response time?

options.text: Computing a true mean over a rolling window is too expensive to do online
It hides how many users actually experienced a given delay
It is distorted by clock skew between the client and the server
It cannot be meaningfully aggregated across several machines

questions.explanation: It is not a good metric for your typical response time. Option d is the trap: that objection is true of percentiles, not of averages. The chapter also notes pedantically that 'average' does not refer to any particular formula, but colloquially means the arithmetic mean.

questions.question: A user's page load issues 4 backend requests. What is the probability that at least one of them is slower than the median?
questions.explanation: 1 minus 0.5 to the fourth power, which is 93.75%. The median refers to a single request, so a user who makes several requests is very likely to hit a slow one — which is why high percentiles matter.

questions.question: Your 95th percentile response time is 1.5 seconds. Exactly what does that mean?

options.text: The average request takes about 1.5 seconds to complete
95 in 100 requests finish faster than 1.5 seconds; 5 in 100 take longer
95% of your users experience a response time of about 1.5 seconds
The slowest request in the measurement window took 1.5 seconds

questions.explanation: High percentiles (p95, p99, p999) are thresholds on the distribution's tail — they tell you how bad the outliers are.

questions.question: Amazon specifies internal service response times at the 99.9th percentile, affecting only 1 in 1,000 requests. What is the reasoning?

options.text: It is the cheapest percentile to compute on a live dashboard
It is the percentile least distorted by garbage collection pauses
The slowest requests belong to the accounts with the most data, the best customers
Financial regulators require reporting at that particular percentile

questions.explanation: They have the most data on their accounts because they have made many purchases. Keeping response times fast for them directly affects users' experience of the service, and therefore revenue.

questions.question: Which figures are cited for the cost of slowness? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: A 100 ms increase in response time reduces sales by 1%
A 1-second slowdown reduces a customer satisfaction metric by 16%
A 10 ms increase doubles the bounce rate on landing pages
A 5-second page load loses 90% of mobile users outright

questions.explanation: Amazon's own observation, plus a reported figure on customer satisfaction.

questions.question: Amazon optimizes p999 but deemed p9999 not worth it. For which two reasons? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Those response times are easily affected by random events outside your control
The benefits of further reduction are diminishing
Histogram approximation algorithms cannot estimate it accurately
Customers do not notice delays that far out in the tail

questions.explanation: Reducing response times at very high percentiles was judged too expensive and to not yield enough benefit.

questions.question: Define SLO and SLA per the chapter.

options.text: SLOs are internal targets; SLAs are contracts that may entitle customers to refunds
SLOs are the contracts with customers; SLAs are the internal dashboards
SLOs constrain availability; SLAs constrain response time percentiles
They are two names for the same document, used in different industries

questions.explanation: Example clauses: a median response time under 200 ms and a p99 under 1 s, and the service considered up at least 99.9% of the time. The definition of 'up' matters, since if the response time is longer, it might as well be down.

questions.question: An SLA promises the service is up at least 99.9% of the time. How much downtime does that permit in a 30-day month?

options.text: 4.3 minutes
43.2 minutes
7.2 hours
8.6 minutes

questions.explanation: 30 days is 43,200 minutes; 0.1% of that is 43.2 minutes.

questions.question: Why do queueing delays dominate high percentiles, and what practical consequence follows?

options.text: A few slow requests block those queued behind them, so measure on the client side
The network dominates the delay, so measure on the server side instead
Collection pauses are periodic, so average over a much longer window
Disk seeks dominate, so the fix is a caching layer in front of storage

questions.explanation: Head-of-line blocking: a server can only process a small number of things in parallel, so even fast requests behind a slow one wait. Server-side measurement would miss that wait.

questions.question: When artificially generating load to test scalability, what must the client-side load generator do?

options.text: Throttle itself as responses slow, to avoid overloading the system under test
Keep sending independently of response time, or queues stay artificially short
Send from a single thread, so that the test is exactly reproducible
Reproduce the production read-to-write ratio as closely as possible

questions.explanation: A generator that waits for the previous response before sending the next one keeps the queues shorter in the test than in reality, which skews the measurements — hiding exactly the queueing effect you are trying to measure.

questions.question: You want percentiles on a monitoring dashboard. Which aggregation is wrong, and what is right?

options.text: Averaging percentiles is meaningless; add the histograms instead
Summing percentiles is wrong; average them across machines instead
Rolling windows distort percentiles; use fixed windows instead
p999 is too noisy to display; report p99 on dashboards instead

questions.explanation: The naive implementation keeps a list of response times in a rolling window and sorts it every minute; if that is too inefficient, use approximation algorithms such as forward decay, t-digest, or HdrHistogram.

questions.question: How often must a fast-growing service revisit its architecture?

options.text: At least once a year, as part of regular capacity planning
On every order of magnitude of load increase, or perhaps more often
Only once an SLA has actually been breached in production
Never, provided the original design was done correctly

questions.explanation: An architecture appropriate for one level of load is unlikely to cope with 10 times that load. Scalability is a moving target, not a property you design in once.

questions.question: Define scaling up and scaling out, and give the verdict on the dichotomy.

options.text: Up adds machines, out adds CPUs to a machine; scaling out always wins
Up suits stateless services, out suits stateful ones; never combine them
Up is a more powerful machine, out is many smaller ones; mix both in practice
Up is elastic, out is manual; the elastic option is always better

questions.explanation: Scaling up is vertical scaling; scaling out is horizontal scaling, also called a shared-nothing architecture. Good architectures usually involve a pragmatic mixture of both: a few fairly powerful machines can be simpler and cheaper than a large number of small virtual machines.

questions.question: When is an elastic system useful, and what is the argument for manual scaling?

options.text: Elastic suits unpredictable load; manual is simpler with fewer surprises
Elastic is always preferable; manual scaling is a legacy practice
Elastic suits predictable load; manual scaling suits spiky load
Elastic is cheaper to run; manual scaling is the more reliable option

questions.explanation: Elastic means automatically adding resources on detecting a load increase; the trade-off is operational predictability. Rebalancing partitions is where the chapter picks this up again.

questions.question: Why is distributing a stateless service easy while distributing a stateful data system is not, and what 'common wisdom' followed?

options.text: Stateless services need consensus, so the wisdom was to shard databases early
Distributing state adds much complexity, so keep the database on one node
Stateful systems cannot be replicated, so the wisdom was to avoid databases
Stateless services are slower, so the wisdom was to cache aggressively

questions.explanation: Keep your database on a single node (scale up) until scaling cost or high-availability requirements force you to distribute it. The chapter notes this wisdom is changing as distributed data system tools and abstractions improve.

questions.question: What is 'magic scaling sauce', and does it exist?

options.text: A generic one-size-fits-all scalable architecture, which does not exist
Twitter's proprietary technique for handling celebrity fan-out
A caching layer that makes any read-heavy system scale linearly
The standard combination of sharding plus asynchronous replication

questions.explanation: The architecture of systems that operate at large scale is usually highly specific to the application. The problem may be the volume of reads, of writes, of data to store, the complexity of the data, the response time requirements, the access patterns, or some mixture.

questions.question: Compare a system designed for 100,000 requests/sec of 1 kB each with one for 3 requests/min of 2 GB each. What follows?

options.text: The first has 100x the throughput, so it needs roughly 100x the machines
The second is the easier system, because it handles far fewer requests
Both move about 100 MB/s, yet the two systems look nothing alike
Throughput is the only load parameter that matters for either system

questions.explanation: 100,000 x 1 kB/s is 100 MB/s; 3 x 2 GB/min is 6 GB/min, also 100 MB/s. Identical on that metric, utterly different in design — so throughput alone does not determine architecture.

questions.question: A scalable architecture assumes which operations are common and which are rare. What should an early-stage product do about that?

options.text: Design for a thousand times the expected load from the first release
Wrong assumptions waste the effort, so iterate quickly on product features
Pick a NoSQL database early, to keep the scaling options open
Hire a dedicated scalability team before the product launches

questions.explanation: If those assumptions are wrong the scaling effort is at best wasted and at worst counterproductive; iterating on features beats scaling to some hypothetical future load. Even so, scalable architectures are built from general-purpose building blocks arranged in familiar patterns.

questions.question: Where does the cost of software actually live?

options.text: Most cost is initial development, so ship fast and rewrite later
Most cost is infrastructure and hosting rather than people
Most cost is testing, which is why it is the first thing cut
Most cost is ongoing maintenance, not the initial development

questions.explanation: Maintenance means fixing bugs, keeping systems operational, investigating failures, adapting to new platforms, modifying for new use cases, repaying technical debt, and adding new features. This is why the chapter treats maintainability as a first-class concern.

questions.question: Why is it hard to give general recommendations for dealing with legacy systems?

options.text: Every legacy system is unpleasant differently, so aim not to create one
Legacy systems are always undocumented, so no general advice applies
A full rewrite is always the answer, so there is nothing to recommend
Legacy maintenance lies outside the scope the book sets for itself

questions.explanation: Instead of general advice it concludes we should design to minimize pain during maintenance. The three design principles — operability, simplicity, evolvability — are the chapter's answer to 'how do I not create one of these?'

questions.question: The chapter defines simplicity as 'make it easy for new engineers to understand the system, by removing as much complexity as possible'. Which clarification does it attach?

options.text: That this is not the same as simplicity of the user interface
That simplicity requires reducing functionality
That simplicity must be traded off against reliability
That simplicity only applies to code, not to data models

questions.explanation: Internal simplicity for engineers, not surface simplicity for users. The chapter also notes evolvability goes by other names: extensibility, modifiability, or plasticity.

questions.question: Explain the quoted claim that 'good operations can often work around the limitations of bad (or incomplete) software, but good software cannot run reliably with bad operations', and the caveat about automation.

options.text: Operations should be fully automated, removing humans from the loop
Operations is load-bearing; humans must still set up and check the automation
Bad software cannot be rescued by any amount of operational skill
Good automation makes a dedicated operations team unnecessary

questions.explanation: Some operational aspects can and should be automated, but it is still up to humans to set up that automation in the first place and to make sure it's working correctly. Automation does not remove the human, it relocates the human's job.

questions.question: Which responsibility of a good operations team is about the organization rather than the machines?

options.text: Monitoring the health of the system and quickly restoring service
Preserving the organization's knowledge as individual people come and go
Keeping software and platforms up to date, including security patches
Establishing good practices for deployment and configuration management

questions.explanation: The list of ten includes tracking down causes, keeping platforms patched, watching how systems affect each other, anticipating problems, and defining processes that make operations predictable.

questions.question: Which ways can data systems make routine operational tasks easy? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Providing visibility into runtime behaviour and internals, with good monitoring
Avoiding dependency on individual machines, so machines can be taken down
Behaving predictably, with good defaults that administrators can still override
Hiding all configuration knobs, so operators cannot set anything incorrectly

questions.explanation: Also on the list: self-healing where appropriate, but giving administrators manual control over the system state. Note two deliberate pairs of opposites — good defaults plus freedom to override, and self-healing plus manual control. Removing control is not on the list.

questions.question: What is a 'big ball of mud', and which are the symptoms of complexity? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Explosion of the state space, and tight coupling of modules
Tangled dependencies, and inconsistent naming and terminology
Hacks aimed at performance, and special-casing to work around issues
Slow build times and unusually large deployment artifacts

questions.explanation: 'Big ball of mud' is the chapter's term for a project mired in complexity. Build times are not among its symptoms. Complexity also slows down everyone working on the system, further increasing cost of maintenance.

questions.question: Why does complexity increase the risk of bugs, not merely slow people down?

options.text: Hidden assumptions and unexpected interactions get overlooked more easily
More lines of code mean proportionally more defects per release
Complex systems resist automated testing, so bugs escape to production
Complex systems tend to attract less experienced engineers

questions.explanation: When the system is harder to understand and reason about, hidden assumptions, unintended consequences, and unexpected interactions are more easily overlooked. The mechanism is cognitive, not statistical — which is why simplicity is treated as a reliability measure.

questions.question: Give Moseley and Marks' definition of accidental complexity, and why the chapter stresses that simplifying does not necessarily mean reducing functionality.

options.text: Complexity introduced by a bug that nobody has yet found and fixed
Complexity not inherent in the problem as users see it, only in the implementation
Complexity that arrives with third-party dependencies you did not write
Complexity that only becomes visible once the system is under load

questions.explanation: Removing it therefore costs no loss of features. The distinction blocks the lazy objection that we must cut scope to simplify.

questions.question: Why is abstraction the best tool for removing accidental complexity, and what is the second-order benefit?

options.text: It reduces the number of lines of code, cutting bugs proportionally
It removes layers of indirection, which makes the system run faster
It hides detail behind a clean facade and is reusable, so fixes benefit every user
It lets a smaller team maintain the same amount of functionality

questions.explanation: A good abstraction can be reused across a wide range of different applications, and reuse also leads to higher-quality software, as quality improvements in the abstracted component benefit all applications that use it. The second-order benefit is the one people forget: fixes flow to every consumer.

questions.question: What does SQL abstract?

options.text: Machine code, CPU registers and operating system calls
On-disk and in-memory structures, concurrent clients, and post-crash inconsistency
Network protocols, serialization formats and wire compatibility
Schema evolution, data migrations and rolling upgrades

questions.explanation: High-level programming languages are what abstract machine code, CPU registers and syscalls. The chapter's point: we are still using machine code, we are just not using it directly, because the abstraction saves us from having to think about it.

questions.question: The chapter does not claim abstraction is a solved technique. What does it admit, specifically about distributed systems?

options.text: Good abstractions are hard to find, and distributed systems lack good packaging
Distributed systems need only good algorithms, not new abstractions
Every abstraction leaks under load, so they are best avoided entirely
SQL already provides the right abstraction for distributed systems

questions.explanation: Though many good algorithms exist, it is much less clear how we should be packaging them into abstractions that keep complexity manageable. Good algorithms are not the bottleneck; packaging them is.

questions.question: Agile already offers TDD and refactoring. Why is 'evolvability' needed as a separate word?

options.text: Agile methods do not apply to data systems in any form
Refactoring addresses only code style, never system structure
Evolvability is nonfunctional, whereas agility is a functional requirement
Those techniques work at a small local scale; a larger system needs its own word

questions.explanation: TDD and refactoring were mostly developed at the scale of a couple of source files within one application; evolvability names agility at the level of a data system of several applications or services. Same idea, different altitude.

questions.question: The chapter closes by splitting requirements into two kinds. Which of the following does it classify as nonfunctional? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Security and reliability
Compliance and scalability
Compatibility and maintainability
Storing, retrieving, searching and processing data

questions.explanation: Functional requirements are what the application should do — store, retrieve, search and process data. Everything else is nonfunctional. And the chapter warns there is unfortunately no easy fix for making applications reliable, scalable, or maintainable.

questions.question: How are faults classified, and which sentence links scalability back to reliability?

options.text: Hardware, software and human faults; scalable systems add capacity to stay reliable
Transient, permanent and Byzantine faults; reliability is a prerequisite for scale
Network, disk and CPU faults; scalability and reliability are independent concerns
Detected and undetected faults; high load always reduces reliability

questions.explanation: 'In a scalable system, you can add processing capacity in order to remain reliable under high load.' Fault-tolerance techniques can hide certain types of faults from the end user. Maintainability is about making life better for the engineering and operations teams.
